Writing NormalizeTest class...

So Node, Compiler, NodeTraversor, and JSDocInfo are all part of the project's own source tree, compiled alongside Normalize.java, so tests can reference them directly without extra jars. The jarjared naming is just about shading to avoid classpath conflicts, while the listed jars (guava, protobuf, args4j) are third-party dependencies used internally by the project itself.

But I'm uncertain whether CompilerTestCase actually exists in this codebase with the API I'd expect -- since the instructions warn against guessing behavior not confirmed in the provided source, relying on an unlisted helper class like that is risky. It's safer to write tests at a lower method level rather than depend on an unconfirmed test harness class.

A more limited approach might be building Node trees manually or using Compiler.parseTestCode directly, then invoking the target methods. But many of those methods are private or nested inside private static classes, making them hard to call without reflection.

Though shouldTraverse/visit are public overrides of Callback interface methods, so they could be invoked through NodeTraversal.traverse. Given the constraint to only use JUnit4 and provided jars, I'm weighing whether to write a comprehensive test suite in that idiom, adding comments flagging assumptions about existing test infrastructure like test() and testSame() methods that are canonical in this codebase.

Since only Normalize.java was provided, I'm considering testing directly against its public API—the static parse methods and the process() method—which requires constructing a real Compiler instance since AbstractCompiler is abstract.

The concrete Compiler class lets me parse code with parseTestCode or parseSyntheticCode, run Normalize's process() on the resulting AST, then verify the output through toSource() or Node.toString(), all using only classes within the project itself.

I'm sketching out several test cases: splitting comma-separated var declarations into separate statements, hoisting for-loop initializers, converting while loops into for loops, and checking constant-by-convention annotation for uppercase variable names.

Tracing through the loop with var x then g: since var x isn't a function declaration, previous gets set to var x, then current advances to g, which is a function declaration, so it removes g and reinserts it at the front using insertAfter (which was null), placing g before var x.

So insertAfter remains fixed at the value captured before the second loop even runs, since it's only reassigned when a function declaration gets moved - meaning it only tracks the leading run of consecutive hoisted declarations from the very start, not anything encountered afterward.

This means g ends up hoisted ahead of var x entirely, matching the intended semantics described in the comment: functions get moved to the very beginning of the scope, only "settling in" after other functions already sitting at the top. So the normalized order becomes function g first, then var x - a genuine behavior worth writing a test for, either by comparing toSource() output or inspecting the node tree to confirm g is the first child.

For the third test, I'm checking how a while loop gets converted into a FOR node, with empty placeholder children inserted around the condition and body to match the standard for-loop shape.

The original WHILE node has just two children: condition and body. So inserting the empty node before the condition and another empty clone after it gives four children total: empty, expr, empty2, body, which then maps onto the FOR node's expected structure of init, condition, increment, body.

Now I want to verify this concretely: the top-level node should be Token.FOR, its first child EMPTY, then the original condition expression, then another EMPTY, then the body.

I also need to consider whether the traversal order (pre-order shouldTraverse vs post-order visit) causes the FOR node to be reprocessed by the initializer extraction logic after the WHILE-to-FOR conversion happens.

Since shouldTraverse for the parent block runs before children are processed, it only sees the WHILE type and skips it; the FOR conversion happens later in post-order visit(), so extractForInitializer never gets a chance to run on the newly created FOR node, and since its init is empty anyway there's nothing to conflict with. Traversal doesn't revisit the parent afterward, so no re-processing occurs.

Now for annotateConstantsByConvention on the condition's NAME node -- since children are visited before parents in post-order, when that NAME node is visited its parent is still typed WHILE, not yet converted to FOR, so any type check on the parent at that moment sees WHILE.
